accuracy.reason: All eight card objectives are supported: cost/benefit, actor-owned reads/fills and keys, stale refill, expiration/eviction, cache placement and bounded fallback. No unconditional freshness claim. Both diagram meanings match prose.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.

mechanisms.reason: Read/miss actors, overlapping reader/writer sequence, separate instance copies and concurrent refill reduction are explained causally; learner transfers them to new domains.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: Repeated product reads develop into ownership, updates, lifetime, placement, failures and the final cache/no-cache decision. Required prerequisites are given or introduced before use.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.

decisions.reason: Balances latency/source savings against copy management, stale values, network dependency and capacity. Freshness-sensitive work checks authoritative data; low-reuse workloads can omit caching.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Plain examples and defined terms explain the eight objectives without an unexplained coordination protocol; concise diagrams distinguish hit/miss and stale source/copy.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

outcomes.reason: C1: repeated expensive guides become reusable. C2: station and language key. C3: hit avoids source. C4: application fetches/stores/returns on miss. C5: application owns cache-aside and miss still pays database plus cache work; exact slides 1-3 support each.

C1: C receives old hours. C2: A refills after deletion using already fetched data. C3: rejects post-write freshness guarantee. C4: bypasses cache for authoritative read, supported by slide 4 and declared commit prerequisite.

C1: 12:03 stale hit, 12:11 source fetch. C2: 12:05 miss after early eviction. C3: TTL neither retains entry nor tracks updates. C4: expiration/eviction distinct and later reader reloads; slides 2/5 support all.

C1: other local copies remain old. C2: chooses single shared entry under no-concurrent-fill assumption. C3: local process versus network lookup. C4: operating/network cost and no automatic freshness. C5: one local loss versus all shared-cache users losing access; does not equate access loss with request failure. Slides 4/6 support all.

C1: concurrent misses multiply source reads. C2: one lookup shared by waiting readers. C3: 10000 exceeds 500 by 20x. C4: cap database admissions and reject excess, sufficient without stale data. C5: optional stale copy explicitly conditional on accessibility and 60-second allowance, never read from failed cache; no invented stale mechanism needed for chosen rejection strategy.

C1-2: rejects cache because unique single reads cannot reuse fills. C3: cheap read and ample headroom. C4: writes/memory/management cost. C5: reconsider repeated IDs with meaningful latency/capacity pressure; slides 1/8 support all.

sourceChecks.claim: Reusable copies save repeated source work but consume memory and fills; Microsoft guidance supports benefit/cost.
Microsoft cache-aside steps match application lookup, fetch, fill and return; hits may be stale.
Application-owned cache-aside and keys distinguishing answer-changing inputs are consistent with Microsoft caching guidance.

Separate source write/invalidation does not guarantee consistency (Microsoft cache-aside). Delayed pre-write fetch can refill after deletion by the stated ordering; diagram correctly shows independent stale copy.
Redis documents memory eviction, LRU and noeviction rejection; TTL expiry differs from capacity removal and neither is a source fetch.
AWS describes independent process copies versus an external shared service and common outage/operating costs.
AWS discusses request coalescing and cache-outage downstream overload; limiting fallback work avoids treating the database as unlimited.
Microsoft guidance makes reuse, source expense and freshness central to cache adoption; lesson appropriately rejects unhelpful caches.
